implementation_notes: C ships no timeout abstraction, so each call site chooses a mechanism: setsockopt(fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_RCVTIMEO, &tv, sizeof tv) makes a blocking socket call give up after the struct timeval and report EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK; poll()/select() take a millisecond budget; pthread_cond_timedwait bounds a condition wait and returns ETIMEDOUT; alarm()/SIGALRM is the process-wide fallback. Nothing replaces the classic structure here, so the timer, the wait and the classification of the expiry are all hand-written; the real decisions are to compute the deadline from CLOCK_MONOTONIC, to keep the timeout distinguishable from every other errno, and to retry EINTR without restarting the budget.
pitfalls: SO_RCVTIMEO/SO_SNDTIMEO report expiry as EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK, and they cover only socket syscalls (accept, connect, read, recvmsg, send, sendmsg): select, poll and epoll_wait ignore them, and name resolution gets no budget at all.
A zero timeval means 'never time out' (the default), so a zeroed or unset timeval silently disables the budget.

pthread_cond_timedwait takes an absolute time with the same origin as time(2)/gettimeofday: a wall-clock step ends the wait early or extends it, and its ETIMEDOUT return must leave the loop instead of being retried like a spurious wakeup.
alarm()/SIGALRM is per-process: in a threaded program the signal interrupts an arbitrary unblocked thread, so it cannot serve as a per-thread deadline.
